studies.title: Praise In Both Homes
studies.meaning: The surah opens by assigning praise twice, and the second assignment is the unexpected one. Praise belongs to God here, because everything in the heavens and the earth is His, and praise belongs to Him in the hereafter as well. The commentators note that no reason is supplied for the second, so it stands as a statement about a place rather than an argument about ownership. Two names close the ayah, one about judgement and one about knowledge of small things.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, opening a surah that will spend most of its length on the objection that a resurrection is impossible. The praise assigned to the hereafter in the first line is therefore doing work before any argument begins: the destination the audience denies is described as already full of praise. Commentators report no particular occasion and read the opening as setting the surah's terms.

keyTerms.note: Praise given for what something is rather than only for what it has done, which distinguishes it from thanks. The definite article makes it the whole category, so nothing is left over to assign elsewhere.
From a root that gives both wisdom and judgement, and also the bridle that governs an animal. The name joins knowing what is right to having the standing to settle it.
One who knows the inner condition of a thing rather than its surface, from a root used of testing soil by ploughing it. It names knowledge acquired by penetration rather than by observation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Praise in Arabia was a public transaction with a market rate. Poets were paid to compose it, and a chief's reputation was built and destroyed in verse that travelled with the caravans. Everyone knew that praise followed power and generosity, and that it moved when they moved. An opening that assigns all of it in one direction, in both worlds, was a claim in a familiar and competitive currency.
studies.didYouKnow: Five surahs of the Quran open with this phrase of praise, and two of them stand side by side in the Book, this one and the one immediately after it. The classical commentators note the pairing, and observe that each of the five then turns to a different ground for the praise it opens with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Extending praise into the hereafter makes a claim about continuity. What is due to God now is not a response to present circumstances that a change of circumstances could revise; it belongs to Him in a world the audience has not seen. The two closing names then attach that to a specific pairing: the one who settles matters is also the one who knows what is inside them, so judgement rests on knowledge rather than on power.

crossReferences.why: Opens the very next surah with the same phrase and grounds it in the making of the angels.
Shows praise actually being given in the hereafter, in the mouths of those who arrive.
Uses the same opening and grounds the praise in a Book sent down without crookedness.

studies.applyIt: Try separating praise from thanks once today. Thanks is for what you received; praise is for what something is, whether or not it went your way. Say one sentence of the second kind before you go to sleep, about God rather than about your circumstances. Most people find the second sentence considerably harder to compose than the first.

studies.title: What Goes In And Comes Out
studies.meaning: Four movements are listed and they make a closed circuit: into the earth, out of it, down from the sky, back up into it. The commentators note that nothing is left outside the four, since anything that moves at all does one of them. What follows is not a name about power, which the list would lead a reader to expect, but two names about mercy and forgiveness. The knowledge is total and the response attached to it is not.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the head of a surah arguing for a resurrection against people who found the idea absurd. The commentators connect this ayah to that argument: a body dispersed into the earth is covered by the first two items in the list. No occasion is reported. The ayah's function is to establish the scope of God's knowledge before the objection is raised a few lines later.

keyTerms.note: A verb for going into something through a narrow opening, the root behind the word for a doorway. It covers rain soaking down and seeds pushed under, entry that is not easily observed.
A verb of stepped rising rather than instant transfer, the same word used of deeds and affairs returning upward. It completes the circuit by making the fourth movement the reverse of the third.
From a root meaning to cover something over, as a helmet covers a head. Placed after a list of what nothing hides from, it says that seeing everything and covering it over are not opposites.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in that economy depended on things going in and coming out of the ground where nobody could watch. A well was dug on a guess about water below. Seed was sown and left. Rain fell somewhere upstream and arrived days later down a dry valley. People lived by making confident decisions about processes they could not observe, which is exactly the kind of knowledge this ayah is describing.
studies.didYouKnow: The two names at the end of this ayah appear in the reverse of their usual order, mercy before forgiveness, where the Quran ordinarily gives forgiveness first. The classical commentators discuss such reversals carefully, since the order in these paired names is consistent enough across the Book that a variation is treated as deliberate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Comprehensive knowledge is usually deployed in scripture as a warning, and here it is followed immediately by two names of leniency. That pairing says something specific: what is known completely can still be covered over, and the covering is not ignorance. It also supplies the ground for the surah's argument about resurrection, since scattering is only a problem for someone who has to find things again.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same four movements in the same order, and adds that He is with you wherever you are.
Extends the same total knowledge down to a falling leaf and a seed in the dark.
Applies this knowledge directly to the resurrection, saying what the earth takes away is known.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing happening out of your sight this week: a decision being made about you, someone's health, a message you sent and heard nothing back about. This ayah lists exactly that category and then names mercy. Say the ayah's two closing qualities over that one situation tonight, rather than rehearsing the possible outcomes again.

studies.title: Not An Atom's Weight Escapes
studies.meaning: A denial is quoted and then answered with an oath, which is rare. The Prophet is told to swear by his Lord that the Hour will come, and then the argument shifts from the promise to the record. Nothing of the smallest weight in the heavens or the earth slips away from Him, nothing smaller and nothing larger, and all of it is in a clear register. The commentators note that this answers the real objection, which is not about time but about whether anything survives to be raised.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The denial quoted here was the standing position of the audience and appears in this surah more than once. Commentators report no single occasion and treat the exchange as representative. The oath is significant to them: the Quran instructs an oath in only a handful of places, and each of them concerns the resurrection or the truth of the message itself.

keyTerms.note: A particle used only to contradict a negative statement, so it cannot begin a sentence on its own. Its presence means the ayah is answering something already said rather than making a fresh claim.
A verb for being far off and out of reach, used of a man who lives away from his people. Negated here, it says nothing is at that kind of distance from God's knowledge.
The smallest thing the language had a word for, understood as a speck of dust in a sunbeam or a small ant. It marks the limit of what a person could notice at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Weight was the great instrument of Meccan commerce. Gold and silver were weighed rather than counted, and disputes turned on the accuracy of a scale and the honesty of the man holding it. Traders knew that below a certain weight nothing could be measured at all. To speak of what is smaller than the smallest measurable thing was to speak past the end of the finest instrument anyone owned.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about a mote's weight occurs six times in the Quran, and two of them are in this surah, here and about twenty ayat later. Two more are the closing lines of a very short surah near the end of the Book, where the same measure is applied to good and to evil in consecutive ayat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah moves the argument from possibility to record. Whether a scattered body could be reassembled is a question about power; whether anything of it is still known is a question about knowledge, and the Quran chooses the second. That makes the resurrection a matter of retrieval from a register rather than of reconstruction from remains, which is a substantially easier thing for a listener to accept.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same measure of a mote's weight to good and to evil in two consecutive lines.
Uses the same phrase and adds that all of it is in a clear register.
Answers the same objection about decayed bones by pointing back to the first creation.

studies.applyIt: Think of the smallest thing you did this week that nobody noticed, good or otherwise. Not a decision, just a moment. This ayah says the register goes down past that. Hold one such moment in mind for thirty seconds tonight. The point is not to feel watched; it is to notice that your own record of your week is far shorter than the actual week.

studies.title: That He May Recompense Them
studies.meaning: A purpose is attached to the register described a moment earlier: the record is kept so that recompense can be given. Two outcomes follow and their vocabulary is not parallel. The first pairs forgiveness with a generous provision, so what is offered exceeds what is owed. The second describes people striving against the signs and names their punishment with a word for a foul affliction. The commentators note that only one of the two sides is described as more than earned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on the oath that the Hour will come and the statement that nothing escapes the record. The surah is answering an audience that treated the resurrection as an absurdity. These two ayat supply the reason such a record would be kept at all, which the commentators read as the missing step in the objectors' own reasoning.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to give what suffices as a return, the same root behind the word for a full settlement. It implies proportion, which is what makes the addition of forgiveness in the next clause notable.

A participle from a verb meaning to render someone unable. It describes people acting to make the message fail rather than merely disagreeing with it, which is why the ayah treats them as a separate category.
A word used in the Quran for the afflictions sent on earlier peoples, carrying a sense of filth and disturbance together. It is harsher than the ordinary term for punishment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Settlement of accounts was a public event in Mecca. When a caravan returned, shares were calculated in front of witnesses, and everyone knew who had put in capital, who had guarded, and who had merely lent a name. A settlement that came out exactly right was expected; a settlement that came out generous was remembered and talked about for years. The two ayat here use exactly that difference.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the punishment in the second of these ayat is the one the Quran uses of afflictions sent upon earlier communities, such as the plagues described in the accounts of Egypt. Its root carries both filth and agitation, so it names a punishment that unsettles as well as harms, which is why it is rarer than the ordinary term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The asymmetry is the point. Recompense implies exactness, and the ayah then breaks its own frame on one side only, adding forgiveness and a generous provision to what proportion would have required. Justice is therefore not presented as the final word about God's dealing, only as the floor beneath it. The second ayah, by contrast, stays inside the proportional frame it was given.

crossReferences.why: Names the same excess, a reward given in full and then increased from His bounty.
Sets out the same two outcomes in the same order, using nearly identical wording.
States the principle behind the asymmetry: no injustice at all, and good deeds doubled.

studies.applyIt: Notice how rarely anyone gives you more than the arrangement required, and how well you remember the times somebody did. Do that once this week in a small way, where nobody has asked and nothing obliges you. This passage puts generosity above exactness rather than beside it, and the difference is easier to feel than to argue about.

studies.title: Those Given Knowledge See It
studies.meaning: A third group appears, after the believers and after those working against the message. These are described only as having been given knowledge, and what they do is see. The commentators generally read them as people already holding an earlier scripture, though some read the phrase more widely. Two things are then said about what was revealed: that it is the truth, and that it guides towards a path. The path is named by two attributes rather than by a destination.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Communities holding earlier scriptures existed in Arabia and along the trade routes north, and their recognition of the message carried weight in Mecca precisely because they were outsiders to the dispute. The commentators discuss which group is meant and record more than one reading. What they agree on is the argumentative function: an assessment is being cited from people with prior competence.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for seeing with the eyes, used here of a judgement reached. Choosing it over a verb of knowing makes their recognition immediate rather than the conclusion of an argument.
The word covers truth in speech and reality in fact together, and it also names a right that is due. What is being affirmed is therefore correspondence and entitlement in one term.
A passive form, so it names one who is praised rather than one who praises. Pairing it with a name of might makes the path lead towards power that is worth praising, which is not automatic.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccans travelled. The winter caravan went south to Yemen and the summer one north into Syria, and along both routes they met communities that had scriptures, priests and monks who could read. Traders came back with stories and sometimes with questions. A claim that such people recognised the new recitation was therefore checkable by anyone in the audience with a cousin in the caravan business.
studies.didYouKnow: The path in this ayah is identified by two of God's names rather than by a destination, which is unusual. Elsewhere the Quran describes a path by where it leads or by whose path it is. Here the road is named after the character of the one it belongs to, so the description of the route and the description of God are the same sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Recognition is attributed to people with prior training, which says something about how evidence works. Knowledge does not create the truth of what is revealed, but it equips a person to recognise it, and the ayah puts that recognition in the vocabulary of sight rather than of argument. The two closing names then define the direction of travel by a character rather than by a place, which keeps guidance from being purely instrumental.

crossReferences.why: Describes those given knowledge before it falling prostrate when the recitation reaches them.
Reports people who had received scripture earlier saying they believed in this before it came.
Cites as witness those who possess knowledge of the Book, against a charge of invention.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone who knows a field you do not, and how quickly they can tell whether something in it is sound. That speed is what this ayah is describing. Spend twenty minutes this week learning one thing properly rather than reading five things quickly. Recognition of the kind the ayah names is built out of exactly that.

studies.title: Shall We Point You To A Man
studies.meaning: The objection is quoted as it was actually said, and its form is a joke. Shall we show you someone, they say, and the word used is simply a man, with no name and no title. What he claims is then repeated back in the most physical terms available: once you have been torn completely to pieces, you will be in a new creation. The commentators note that the mockery does the work of an argument, which is why the Quran preserves the wording rather than summarising it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a period of open ridicule rather than of debate. The commentators describe the resurrection as the single point on which the Meccan audience found the message most implausible, more than the claim about God's oneness. No particular occasion is reported for this ayah, which is read as a representative sample of how the message was being repeated in the city.

keyTerms.note: A verb for guiding someone to a thing they are looking for, ordinarily used of directing a traveller. Its polite, helpful register is exactly what makes the sentence mocking.
Indefinite and unqualified, which is the insult. Refusing a name or a description reduces the person to a category, and the Quran preserves the reduction rather than correcting it.
An intensive form from a verb for ripping cloth apart. The word occurs twice in the Quran and both times in this surah, first here in mockery and later of what happened to a people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mockery was a recognised instrument in Arabia, more effective in some settings than argument. A satirical verse could travel further than a sermon and lodge in memory better, and men who could compose one were feared. The construction quoted here, offering to introduce someone as a curiosity, is the opening move of that kind of performance, and the audience would have recognised the form at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for being torn to pieces occurs exactly twice in the Quran, and both occurrences are in this surah. Here it is used by objectors mocking the idea of resurrection. Twelve ayat later the same word describes what became of a prosperous people who were scattered until only stories of them remained. The surah answers the joke with its own vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The Quran preserves ridicule directed at its own claim, in the words of those who made it, which is not what a text protecting a reputation would do. It also identifies where the resistance actually lay. Not in the difficulty of believing in God, which this audience largely granted, but in the specific proposal that a person torn apart could be reassembled and held responsible.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same rare word for tearing, of a people scattered until only stories remained.
Quotes the same objection at greater length from an earlier community, in similar mocking terms.
Reports the identical question about bones and fragments, and the answer given to it.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the objection here is delivered as a joke rather than as an argument, and that jokes are harder to answer. When someone dismisses something you hold by making it sound ridiculous, resist the urge to laugh along and resist the urge to argue. Ask them, plainly, what they actually think happens. The question is usually more interesting than the joke was.

studies.title: A Lie Or A Madness
studies.meaning: The mockery finishes with a pair of alternatives offered as though they exhausted the possibilities: either he made this up deliberately, or something has disturbed his mind. The commentators note that the two options are not really symmetrical, since one accuses and the other excuses. Then the ayah answers without addressing either. It says the people who do not believe in the hereafter are already in torment and already far astray, which relocates the affliction they were attributing to him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The two charges quoted here, deliberate invention and disturbance of mind, were the standing explanations offered in the city for what was being recited. Both appear across the Meccan surahs. Commentators report no single occasion and treat the pair as a summary of the available public positions rather than as one person's words on one day.

keyTerms.note: From a root for cutting and stitching material into a new shape. The charge is one of assembly rather than of pure invention, which is why it was the more damaging of the two accusations.
From the root meaning to cover or conceal, the same root behind the word for the unseen beings and for a garden shaded over. Madness in this vocabulary is a covering of the mind.
An adjective of distance attached to the straying, so error is measured as a length rather than as a kind. It says the gap has been growing rather than that a wrong turn was taken once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The charge of being touched was not simply an insult in that society; it was a recognised diagnosis. Poets and soothsayers were held to receive their words from unseen sources, and an association with them was ordinary enough to be a category rather than a slur. Offering it as an alternative to deliberate lying was, in one sense, the more charitable of the two options being put.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for madness comes from the same root as the word for the unseen beings and as the word for a garden. What connects them is covering: a garden is covered over by its foliage, the unseen are concealed from sight, and a mind in this condition is described as having something laid over it. The classical lexicographers treat the root's core sense as concealment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply does not defend the messenger, which is the notable move. It shifts the subject entirely to the accusers and describes their present condition, saying they are in torment now rather than only later. That treats disbelief in a hereafter as something already being suffered rather than as a position with consequences deferred, and it turns the vocabulary of affliction back on the people who had reached for it first.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same charge of madness directly, saying their companion is not touched at all.
Opens a surah by denying the same accusation, and follows it with a great reward.
Puts the same two alternatives, invention or madness, and says he brought them the truth.

studies.applyIt: Notice the shape of the accusation here: two options offered as if there were no third. That move is common and it works by hiding the alternatives rather than refuting them. Next time somebody frames a choice for you in exactly two ways, spend one minute writing down a third before you answer. There usually is one.

studies.title: The Sky Before And Behind
studies.meaning: A question is asked about position rather than about doctrine: have they not looked at what is in front of them and behind them, of sky and of earth. The commentators read the phrasing as saying that the evidence surrounds them in every direction, so no turn of the head escapes it. Then two possibilities are named, the ground opening beneath them or a piece of sky falling on them, and the ayah closes by calling this a sign for one specific kind of person.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the mockery about a body torn to pieces. The commentators read the connection as an argument by scale: people who find one reassembly implausible are standing inside something much larger that they have stopped noticing. No occasion is reported. The surah continues to answer the objection indirectly rather than by taking it on its own terms.

keyTerms.note: A verb for ground swallowing something down, used elsewhere of a man and his house going under. The same root names the eclipse, where light is swallowed rather than earth.
A plural for pieces broken off something larger. Applied to the sky it treats what looks continuous as breakable, which is the unsettling part of the image rather than the falling.
A participle from a verb meaning to return repeatedly to a place. It names habitual returning rather than a single act of repentance, so the sign registers with people already in the habit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabian sky was the most reliable thing in that world and the ground the least. Wells failed, valleys flooded without warning, and the ruins of swallowed settlements lay along the trade routes as ordinary landmarks. Travellers navigated by stars precisely because everything at ground level was uncertain. The ayah reverses that intuition by suggesting the sky is no more permanent than the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The last word of this ayah names a person who habitually turns back, and the same participle recurs seven times in the Quran. Several of those occurrences close a passage by calling something a sign for exactly such a person. The classical commentators read the pattern as saying a sign is not self-enforcing: it registers with someone already in the practice of returning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah says that evidence and disposition are two different things, and it says so in its closing clause rather than as a general principle. The same sky is above everybody. What decides whether it functions as a sign is a habit of turning, which means the argument the surah is making cannot be won by supplying more evidence. That explains the shape of the whole passage, which offers observation rather than proof.

crossReferences.why: Directs the same look at the sky and the earth and ends on one who turns back.
Records a people demanding exactly this, that a piece of the sky be dropped on them.
Describes the ground actually caving in on a man and his dwelling, with nobody to help.

studies.applyIt: Go outside once this week and look up for a full minute, without a phone and without trying to feel anything in particular. This ayah asks for a turn of the head before it asks for anything else. Most people have not looked at the sky attentively in months, and the passage treats that as the actual problem.

studies.title: Iron Softened In His Hands
studies.meaning: A favour is announced and then itemised, and the items are of two kinds. Mountains and birds are told to echo with him, which is a gift of accompaniment rather than of power. Iron is made soft for him, which is a gift of craft. Then an instruction follows, to make coats of mail and measure the links, and it is joined to a second instruction about righteous work. The commentators note the two are given in one breath, so the trade and the character are not separated.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the point where the surah turns from argument to precedent. Having answered mockery about a resurrection, it names two figures who were given extraordinary things and shows what was asked of them. David is remembered in the Quran for judgement, for psalms, and here for metalwork. The commentators read the sequence as showing that favour in the Quran always arrives attached to a task.

keyTerms.note: An imperative from a root meaning to come back repeatedly, used of evening return and of turning to God. Mountains echoing his praise are described as returning it rather than merely making noise.
A plural adjective meaning ample and complete, standing in for the noun. It occurs only here in the Quran, and its sense is armour long enough to cover fully rather than armour merely worn.
A word for joining pieces in sequence, used of chain mail and of continuous narration. The instruction is to get the proportion of the links right, which is a technical rather than a moral direction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Iron was imported, expensive and worked by specialists. A mail coat was among the most valuable objects a man could own, took months to make, and was named and inherited. Rings were cut, bent, overlapped and riveted one at a time, and a coat with links too wide or too thin failed at the worst moment. The instruction about measuring the links is the advice of a craftsman.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the coats of mail occurs only once in the entire Quran, and so do two other words in this surah, one for a staff and one for a dam. The classical commentators explain all three from usage in poetry and ordinary speech rather than from any second occurrence, which is why their discussions of this surah dwell on vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a technical instruction and a moral one in the same sentence, and gives the technical one first. Measuring the links properly is not treated as a lesser matter than working righteousness; it is the immediate content of what was asked. That resists a division most readers bring, in which craft is neutral and character is religious, and the closing clause about being observed covers both together.

crossReferences.why: Names the same craft taught to him, and says it was to protect people from their own violence.
Describes the same mountains and birds joining David in praise at evening and sunrise.
Names iron as sent down, with great strength in it and benefits for people.

studies.applyIt: Take the most technical part of whatever you do, the part you think of as merely skill, and do it carefully once this week. Measure the links. This passage places that instruction beside working righteously without any break between them, which suggests they are closer together than most people's mental filing allows.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: A Month In The Morning
studies.meaning: The wind is described by its working day, and the measurement is the striking part: a morning's run covering a month and an evening's run another month. A spring of molten metal is made to flow, and workers among the unseen beings labour under a leave that is explicitly named. The commentators note the repeated qualification: nothing here is described as the possession of the one who holds it, and a consequence is stated for any of the workers who swerve.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the sequence of favours given to earlier figures. The surah is establishing that extraordinary gifts have been granted before and were always attached to conditions. Commentators discuss the nature of the journeys described and record more than one reading of how the months are counted. What they treat as settled is the framing, in which every item is granted rather than possessed.

keyTerms.note: A noun for the outward going of a day, the departure at first light. It is one half of a pair the Arabic language uses for a complete day, the going out and the coming back.
The other half of the pair, the return journey made in the later part of the day. Together the two words divide a day the way a herdsman or a merchant actually experienced it.
A word for permission granted, from the root meaning to hear and to allow. Its presence turns the whole arrangement into a delegation, which is why a penalty can follow for stepping outside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A month was the standard unit of long travel. The great caravans left in a season and returned in a season, and everyone measured distance by how many days of walking or riding it took. To be told that a single morning covered a month's journey was to be told something in a unit the audience used daily. The gift is described in the vocabulary of the trade routes.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for a morning going out appears elsewhere in the Quran paired with a different term for the day's end, in passages about praising God at both edges of a day. Only in this ayah is it set against the word for a homeward journey, so the day is measured the way a traveller experienced it rather than the way a worshipper did.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Every element in this ayah is qualified. The wind is given, the spring is made to flow, the workers labour by leave, and a consequence is named for stepping outside the command. That is a deliberate pattern: what looks like unlimited power is described entirely in the grammar of permission. Sovereignty stays with the one who granted it, and the passage never lets the reader forget where the arrangement came from.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same wind running by his command towards the land God had blessed.
Gives the same gifts of wind and workers, and calls the whole a grant without reckoning.
Has him name what he was taught and given, and calls it a clear favour.

studies.applyIt: Notice how many things in your day arrive with a permission attached that you never think about: the road being open, the power being on, your body doing what you asked. Pick one and name it as borrowed rather than owned, once, when you use it tomorrow. That single qualification is what this whole ayah is built out of.

studies.title: Work In Thankfulness
studies.meaning: A list of what was built, and then a single instruction that reframes all of it. Sanctuaries, figures, basins the size of cisterns, cauldrons too heavy to move: the vocabulary is a workshop inventory. Then the household is told to work in thanks. The commentators note the construction, which makes gratitude the manner or purpose of the labour rather than something said once the labour is done. The closing observation uses an intensive form, so what is called rare is the thankful person rather than the act of thanking.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah sets two histories beside each other. Here a household is given extraordinary means and told what the means are for; a few ayat later a kingdom is given two gardens, turns away, and loses them when a dam breaks. The contrast would land hard in a city that measured divine favour in prosperity and read prosperity as evidence that it was approved of.

keyTerms.note: Wide vessels for communal food, compared here to watering troughs or cisterns for their size. The word belongs to hospitality on a scale where the household is feeding strangers continually.
The word used of mountains anchored in the earth, applied to cooking pots. It means they were never taken down, which says something about the kitchen without describing it.
An intensive form describing a settled disposition rather than an occasional response. The Quran also uses this exact word as a name of God, who is described as appreciative of what people do.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A cauldron too heavy to lift was a public statement in that world. It meant a fire kept going and food available to whoever arrived, which was the highest form of standing a household could hold. Travellers navigated by which houses fed them. Vessels on that scale were listed among a family's assets and remembered in poetry alongside horses and swords.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used at the end of this ayah for a deeply grateful servant is also used in the Quran as a name of God, twice in the following surah, where He is called Forgiving and Appreciative. The same intensive form therefore describes something rare in human beings and constant in the one they are thanking.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Gratitude is presented as a mode of work rather than a form of speech, which places it inside ordinary labour instead of alongside it as a separate observance. The final clause is an observation rather than a threat, and its subject is human beings generally rather than any particular people. Naming the disposition with a word also used of God quietly makes thankfulness a resemblance rather than a payment.

crossReferences.why: Shows a member of the same household asking to be held to exactly what this ayah instructs.
Uses the same intensive word as a name of God, paired with forgiveness, in a description of the Garden.
States the promise attached to thankfulness that gives the instruction here its point.

studies.applyIt: Take one piece of ordinary work you will do today, the kind nobody thanks anyone for, and do it as though it were the thank-you note rather than a task before the thank-you note. Same job, same time. The ayah puts gratitude inside the working rather than after it, and the difference is only findable by trying it.

studies.title: A Creature Ate His Staff
studies.meaning: A death is decreed and nothing announces it. The only thing that eventually reveals it is a creature of the earth working away at the staff he was leaning on, and when the support gives way he falls. The commentators note what the ayah is actually demonstrating: it became clear to the workers that they had not known the unseen, since they had gone on labouring the whole time. The proof of an ignorance is delivered by the smallest agent in the scene.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the account of Solomon that began two ayat earlier. The surah is answering people who mocked a claim about knowledge of what is hidden. This passage supplies a case in which beings famous in that culture for access to concealed things turn out to have had none. Commentators discuss the details of the account and differ on them, while agreeing on the point it is being told to make.

keyTerms.note: A noun from the verb for moving slowly along the ground, covering any small walking animal. Its ordinariness is the point: the agent that exposes the situation is the least significant thing present.
A word for a walking stick, from a root meaning to drive an animal forward or to postpone something. It occurs only here in the Quran, and the classical commentators explain it from ordinary usage.
The verb of falling under one's own weight, the same word used elsewhere of people falling into prostration. It gives no cause beyond gravity, which is what makes the moment so plain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wood was scarce and precious in that country, and everything made of it was slowly attacked from inside. Beams, doors and posts were eaten hollow by insects that left the surface intact until the day the thing gave way. Every household knew the experience of a support that looked sound and was not. The image in this ayah was a piece of ordinary domestic knowledge before it was anything else.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the staff in this ayah occurs only once in the whole Quran, and it is one of three words unique to this surah, alongside a term for coats of mail and one for a dam. Because there is no second occurrence to compare, the classical commentators worked these words out from poetry and common speech instead.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes a claim about hidden knowledge and disproves it with a small animal and a length of wood. Nothing dramatic is required, and no announcement is made. That says something about how such claims usually end: not by being refuted in argument but by simply running out, in a moment nobody staged. The humility being taught is about the limits of what anyone can know, not about anyone's failure.

crossReferences.why: States plainly that the keys of the unseen are with God and nobody else knows them.
Says God discloses His unseen to nobody except a messenger of His choosing.
Tells him to say that nobody in the heavens or the earth knows the unseen but God.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you are currently leaning on without checking: a piece of software, an arrangement at work, an assumption about somebody's availability. Not to become anxious about it. Just look at it once this week, deliberately, the way you would inspect a wooden post. The passage is about supports that fail quietly rather than about disasters.

studies.title: Two Gardens Right And Left
studies.meaning: A whole civilisation is summarised in one sentence, and the sentence describes a sign rather than an empire. Two gardens, one on each side, which the commentators read as cultivation running along both banks of a watered valley. Then a two-part instruction is quoted, to eat and to give thanks, and the ayah closes with a phrase of four words describing land and Lord together. Nothing about power or trade appears, though this people were famous for both.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The kingdom named here lay in the south of the peninsula and was known to every Meccan trader, since the winter caravan went that way. Its great dam and irrigation works were among the wonders of the region, and reports of its decline were current. The commentators treat the audience's familiarity with the place as the reason the surah can invoke it so briefly.

keyTerms.note: From the root for stillness and settling, so a dwelling is where movement stops. Using it of a whole kingdom describes the place as somewhere people had come to rest rather than as a territory held.
A word for an inhabited district rather than for open ground. Its indefinite form here makes the phrase a description offered rather than a name given, which is why it reads like a verdict.
An adjective covering what is pleasant, clean and lawful together. Applied to a land it means fertile and healthy at once, and the same word describes speech, food and a life elsewhere in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The southern kingdom was the far end of the incense road, and Meccan prosperity depended on that traffic. Frankincense and myrrh moved north through Mecca to Syria, and the south was known as the green end of Arabia, with terraced fields and engineered water. For a Meccan audience this was not a legend from the deep past but a place their relatives had traded in.
studies.didYouKnow: The name of this people occurs twice in the Quran, here and in an account of a bird bringing news of them to Solomon. The surah is named after them. The two passages are separated by several surahs and describe the same people at very different moments, once at the height of their standing and once at its end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah gives an entire prosperity a single purpose: it was a sign. Not a reward, not an achievement, and not a neutral fact about geography. Attaching the instruction about thanks directly to the instruction about eating also refuses to make gratitude a separate activity performed afterwards. And the closing phrase pairs the quality of the land with a quality of God, so the gift and the giver are described in one breath.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other mention of this people, reported by a bird returning to Solomon.
States the principle attached here: thankfulness brings increase, and its absence brings the opposite.
Describes a town secure and provided for, which then denied the favours of God.

studies.applyIt: Look at the most ordinary good thing in your week, the one that has become invisible because it never fails. Running water, a working commute, a person who is reliably there. This ayah calls exactly that kind of thing a sign. Name one of them aloud tomorrow morning before you use it, and then use it as usual.

studies.title: The Flood Of The Dam
studies.meaning: Two words carry the turn: they turned away, so We released. What follows is not destruction but substitution, and the detail of the replacement is what makes the passage sting. Two gardens are exchanged for two gardens, with the same count and everything else altered: bitter fruit, tamarisk, and a scattering of thorn trees. The second ayah then names the reason with a word for ingratitude and asks whether any but the ungrateful are dealt with this way.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The failure of the great dam in the south was a known event, remembered in poetry and in the migration stories of tribes who moved north afterwards. The commentators describe the collapse and the dispersal that followed it as the background here. The Quran gives no date, and the audience did not need one, since the consequences had reshaped the tribal map of the peninsula they lived in.

keyTerms.note: A word the classical commentators read as a dam or an embankment, and some as the flood itself. It occurs only here in the Quran, and the range of readings reflects the absence of any second occurrence.
An adjective for fruit that is sour or has turned, food that can be eaten but is not wanted. The replacement is not barrenness but a downgrade, which is a more precise and more humiliating picture.
An intensive form from a root meaning to cover something over. Ingratitude in Arabic is a burying of a favour, and the same root gives the word for denying God, so the two ideas share one term.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water engineering was the difference between a settlement and a desert in that country. A dam or a channel was maintained by generations, and everyone in an oasis knew whose job it was to clear which section. When such works failed, the failure was usually preceded by years of neglect that nobody had wanted to be responsible for. The audience understood exactly how such a thing happens.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the dam occurs only once in the Quran, and the classical commentators record several readings of it: an embankment, a destructive flood, or the name of a valley. Because there is no other occurrence to compare, they set the possibilities side by side without choosing, which is how a good deal of this surah's rarest vocabulary is handled.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The replacement rather than the removal is the theological content. Two gardens are still there, counted the same way, and everything about them has changed. That describes a kind of loss most people recognise better than catastrophe: the outward shape persisting while what made it worth having drains out of it. Ingratitude is then named as the cause, using a word that means covering something over rather than failing to say thanks.

crossReferences.why: Tells at length of two gardens ruined after their owner forgot who had given them.
States the principle this passage illustrates, about thankfulness and its absence.
Describes owners of a garden who planned to withhold its yield and found it stripped.

studies.applyIt: Think of something in your life that still has the same shape as it did five years ago and less of the substance: a friendship kept up by messages, a practice you go through without attention. This passage is about exactly that kind of exchange. Put one hour into the one you name, this week, before the shape is all that is left.

studies.title: Travel By Night And Day
studies.meaning: The favour being described is infrastructure. Towns were placed between them and the blessed lands to the north, close enough to be visible from one another, and the stages of the journey were measured out. Then an instruction is quoted in the imperative: travel among them, nights and days, in safety. The commentators note that the gift is not wealth but the ordinary conditions of movement, the kind of thing a person only notices once it is gone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The incense road ran from the south of the peninsula up through the Hijaz to Syria, and the settlements along it made the journey possible for ordinary traders rather than only for armed expeditions. Commentators describe a chain of towns close enough that a traveller was never far from water and shelter. The Meccan audience worked this road, so the description was current rather than historical.

keyTerms.note: An adjective for what is apparent rather than hidden. Applied to the towns it means each was within sight of the next, so a traveller could always see where the following stage lay.
A verb for apportioning by measure, from the root that gives the word for a determined amount. The stages of a journey are described as set deliberately rather than as falling where they happened to.
A participle from the root that also gives the words for faith and for trust. Security in this vocabulary is the state of being able to rely on something, which is why the same root serves both.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan route was a chain of known stops. Water at this well, a market at that town, a stretch that had to be crossed before dark. Travellers memorised the sequence, and a merchant's competence lay largely in knowing it. Raiding made whole stretches impassable for a season and could ruin a trading family. Safe travel by night was the clearest possible sign that a route was in good order.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction quoted in this ayah names nights before days, which is the reverse of the usual order in Arabic and in the Quran. The classical commentators read the inversion as emphasis: safety at night was the harder half of the claim, since travelling after dark was ordinarily the more dangerous choice, so naming it first makes the point of the whole ayah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The favour named here is not abundance but reliability, which is a different category and a harder one to be grateful for. Nobody notices a road that works. By listing measured stages and visible towns among God's gifts, the passage extends the vocabulary of blessing to include arrangement and order, and the following ayah shows what happens when people become bored with precisely that.

crossReferences.why: Records the response to this arrangement, a request that the journeys be made longer.
Names the two seasonal caravans as a favour, and the security that made them possible.
Points at a secure sanctuary while people around it were being seized, as a favour unnoticed.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list of things that worked today without your attention: the route you took, the water, the lock on your door. Reliability is the one favour that is invisible by design. Read the list once tonight. The ayah after this one is about people who had all of it and asked for something more interesting.

studies.title: Lengthen Our Journeys
studies.meaning: The request is the strangest sentence in the surah. They ask their Lord to put more distance between their journeys, which the commentators read as dissatisfaction with an ease that had become dull, or as a wish for the long hauls that make a merchant's fortune. The ayah adds that they wronged themselves, and then describes the outcome in two images: they were made into stories, and scattered completely. The second ayah names who turned out to have been right about them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The dispersal of the southern tribes after their irrigation failed was a known chapter of Arabian history, and several tribes of the Hijaz and the north traced their arrival to it. Commentators report the request in this ayah as recorded rather than inferred, and they differ over what motivated it, offering both boredom with security and appetite for larger trade.

keyTerms.note: An imperative asking for separation to be increased. Addressed to God as a request, it is one of the few places in the Quran where people are quoted asking for something plainly worse for themselves.
The plural of a word for a report or a piece of news. To be made into it is to survive only as material for other people's conversation, which is a specific and unsettling kind of ending.
An intensive form of the word for patience. It appears four times in the Quran and every time it is paired with the word for one who gives thanks, so the two qualities are treated as one disposition.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Long journeys made large fortunes and destroyed families. A short safe run between neighbouring towns returned a modest, reliable margin, while a season-long haul to Syria could multiply a man's capital or lose him everything, including his sons. Traders argued about this constantly. The request quoted here would have sounded, to a Meccan audience, like a specific and recognisable kind of ambition.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used at the end of this passage for tearing something completely apart occurs only twice in the Quran, and both are in this surah. Twelve ayat earlier, objectors used it while mocking the idea that a body torn to pieces could be raised. Here the same word describes what actually happened to a prosperous people in history.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a failure that has nothing to do with denial or disobedience. What is described is restlessness inside a good arrangement, and the Quran treats it as serious enough to end a civilisation. Naming the outcome as becoming stories also says something about how such endings look from outside: not dramatic, just a people who used to be here and are now something other people mention.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same rare word for being torn apart, there in mockery of the resurrection.
Describes the arrangement this request was asking to have taken away.
Also describes peoples made into stories after their messengers were denied.

studies.applyIt: Notice one good arrangement in your life that you have started finding dull: a steady job, a quiet stretch at home, a friendship without drama. You do not have to feel grateful for it on command. Just name it once as good, out loud, before you next catch yourself wanting something to happen. That is the whole of what this passage asks.

studies.title: Whatever You Spend Is Replaced
studies.meaning: This answers something quoted a few ayat earlier, where people point at their wealth and their sons as proof that nothing will befall them. Provision is described as spread wide or drawn close by a decision, and the decision is explicitly not a verdict on the person. Then a promise: whatever you spend is replaced. The verb is the one used of a successor stepping into the place of the one before, so what is described is substitution rather than repayment, and the currency of the replacement is left unstated.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The preceding ayat quote objectors saying that they have more wealth and more children and will therefore not be punished, and the reply denies that either brings anyone closer. The community hearing this had watched members lose trade and standing for accepting the message, so whether prosperity indicated approval was not a philosophical question for them but a daily one.

keyTerms.note: The verb for unrolling a cloth or opening a hand flat. Provision is pictured as something laid out to a width rather than counted, which is why its opposite in the same sentence is measuring.
From the root of measure and capacity, not of withholding. Restriction is described as an exact allotment rather than a refusal, which removes the sense of a punishment being administered.
From the root that gives the word for a successor. What is promised is something taking the place of what was spent, which is a different claim from the same thing being returned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Mecca was visible and it moved fast. A merchant's capital travelled with a caravan for months, and a household cut out of the trading network by its neighbours lost everything measurable within a season. Giving away goods in that setting was not an abstraction about generosity: it was removing part of the stock that a family's survival through the next year depended on.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for replacing in this ayah comes from the same root as the word used for a successor placed on the earth, and the word for someone who comes after another and takes their position. The promise is therefore worded not as a refund but as a succession: something else steps into the vacancy that the spending made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two ideas that people habitually fuse are separated in consecutive sentences: that provision is distributed by God, which is affirmed, and that its size measures His approval, which is denied. The promise about spending then reverses the arithmetic everyone assumes, that giving is subtraction. Leaving the form of the replacement unstated is deliberate, since naming it would turn the promise into an investment scheme.

crossReferences.why: Names the two voices in the decision: one promising poverty, the other promising forgiveness and bounty.
Puts the same movement as a loan offered to God and multiplied many times over on return.
Shows the regret of someone asking for a short delay in order to give, when the time has run out.

studies.applyIt: Give something away this week at a moment when it is mildly inconvenient rather than comfortable: before payday rather than after, from what you were saving rather than from what was left over. Then watch what actually happens over the following month, without arranging anything to make the ayah come true.
